n0001.title: Towards a Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Bugs are inevitable in any program doing real computation, because computational irreducibility means behavior cannot be foreseen without running it.
n0001.question: Theory of Bugs — why can't bugs be eliminated from programs that do real computation? (an argument with examples)
n0001.sourceHeading: Towards a Theory of Bugs: The Ruliology of the Unexpected

n0002.title: “My Program Did the Wrong Thing!”
n0002.gist: Even very simple programs can do unexpected things, so bugs can be studied scientifically through the unpredictability of computation.
n0002.question: Bugs — can they have a general scientific theory? (a framing of the approach)

n0003.title: Can bugs have a theory
n0003.gist: Bugs are everywhere and each looks unique, yet the essay proposes a general theory built on computational irreducibility, with consequences for testing, verification, security and AI-written code.

n0010.title: Simple programs already have bugs
n0010.gist: A program must stay simple enough to match what we have in mind, but even simple programs can compute in unforeseeable ways, which we then call bugs, and automated bug hunters cannot escape this.

n0015.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0015.gist: Tiny Turing machines that seem to compute n + 1 can hide failures that appear only at large inputs, often those whose binary form is all 1s.
n0015.question: Turing machines — how do hidden bugs show up in tiny programs? (worked examples)

n0016.title: A machine that fails at 7
n0016.gist: A 3-state machine that looks like it adds 1 gives 9 for input 7, and the glitches recur at inputs of the form 8k – 1, where the head scribbles extra digits.

n0029.title: Many correct machines, late bugs
n0029.gist: Thousands of 3-state machines correctly compute n + 1 in varied ways, but counting those that survive up to each n shows some fail only as late as n = 15.

n0043.title: Four-state machines and risky inputs
n0043.gist: Among 4-state machines some bugs wait until n = 63, and the riskiest inputs are those that are all 1s in binary, with the worst bug at n = 2^(2(s–1)) – 1.

n0051.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0051.gist: A bug only exists relative to a specification other than the program itself, and for every kind of specification some machines appear to obey it until they suddenly fail.
n0051.question: Specifications — what makes something count as a bug? (three kinds of specification)

n0052.title: Specifications beyond the program
n0052.gist: A program always does what it does, so bugs arise only against an easier-to-grasp specification, such as a restatement in another language or a second program of the same type.

n0056.title: Two machines that diverge
n0056.gist: Two Turing machines that look like they compute the same function differ suddenly at n = 27, and the places where their outputs differ form a surprisingly complicated pattern.

n0063.title: Forbidden behaviors and output constraints
n0063.gist: Machines can seem to obey a rule such as no unbounded tape use, no infinite loop, or only even outputs, then break it at n = 42, 151 or 32, so some always escape.

n0079.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0079.gist: Cellular automata built to double a block of cells show the same pattern: many rules work, but some fail only at inputs like 14, 24 or 32.
n0079.question: Cellular automata — do they hide late bugs as Turing machines do? (examples)

n0093.title: Can One Tell If There’s Going to Be a Bug?
n0093.gist: Visual simplicity guarantees correctness and visual complexity raises suspicion, but a complicated pattern can still be proven bug-free by seeing how its inner rule works, while others stay undecidable by inspection.
n0093.question: Bug prediction — how can we know whether a program will ever fail? (case studies)
n0093.sourceHeading: Can One Tell If There’s Going to Be a Bug?

n0094.title: Obvious cases and unclear ones
n0094.gist: Some doubling automata plainly stay inside a fixed envelope, but a similar-looking one shows no bug up to n = 100000 while its stabilization time fluctuates randomly with no guarantee.

n0114.title: A proof from the rule’s structure
n0114.gist: In a second case the pattern sits inside a leftward-moving white rind and follows rule 122 inside it, which can never die out, so it must always stabilize and double correctly.

n0129.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0129.gist: Formal symbolic proofs can show simple Turing machines never fail, but searching for a proof costs as much as running cases, and no proof exists when a bug does.
n0129.question: Formal proofs — can they remove the need to test programs? (a worked proof)

n0130.title: Encoding a machine in symbols
n0130.gist: A machine's tape, head and halting behavior can be written as symbolic expressions and algebra-like axioms, reducing the claim that it computes n + 1 for all inputs to one statement with m.

n0157.title: Proving it with induction
n0157.gist: An automated equational proof search, using induction at the end, proves that the machine adds 1 for every input, and similar proofs cover all 17 correct 2-state machines.

n0166.title: No proof for buggy machines
n0166.gist: Proofs are paths in a multiway graph of derivable theorems; for a buggy machine none is ever found, and the search is no cheaper than running cases, though type theory is an alternative.

n0180.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0180.gist: Bugs ultimately come from computational irreducibility, since power and unpredictability go together, but pockets of reducibility let us prove some properties of a program, with proofs lengthening as irreducibility grows.
n0180.question: Computational irreducibility — why does it make bugs unavoidable? (an argument)

n0191.title: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction
n0191.gist: Testing and scientific induction fail wherever irreducibility lurks, because bugs can be arbitrarily rare, and exhaustive sampling in ruliology keeps turning up surprises after thousands to trillions of cases.
n0191.question: Testing — why can't sampling cases show a program has no bugs? (an argument)
n0191.sourceHeading: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction

n0203.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0203.gist: Across cellular automata, Turing machines, combinators and multiway systems, simple rules often behave regularly for a long time before something unexpected happens, so bugs are the rule in ruliology.
n0203.question: Ruliology — how common are sudden surprises in simple systems? (a gallery of examples)

n0235.title: Mathematical “Bugs”
n0235.gist: Mathematics also has counterexamples that appear only astronomically far out, but pure mathematics mostly stays in human-level pockets of reducibility, while experimental mathematics faces the same surprises as ruliology.
n0235.question: Mathematics — why does it rarely hit bugs as ruliology does? (examples and explanation)

n0250.title: Bugs in Practice
n0250.gist: Since bugs cannot be removed outright, the practical defenses are well-designed languages and seeing inside computations, though deeper bugs persist in conventional programs, AI-written code and trained neural nets.
n0250.question: Bugs in practice — how can we best live with unavoidable bugs? (a set of recommendations)

n0251.title: Language design and short programs
n0251.gist: Understanding everything a program does would make it reducible, so the best chance is a well-designed language whose primitives pack irreducible work and make short programs do what humans want.

n0260.title: Seeing inside computations
n0260.gist: Visualizing a computation, as spacetime pictures do for 1D automata, gives confidence beyond formal proof, and the symbolic paradigm lets fragments of a program run alone to reveal it.

n0264.title: Human, AI and neural net bugs
n0264.gist: Human slips and typical errors can be caught by typechecking or AI, but deeper bugs from computation itself remain, and neural nets trained on examples can always spurt out unexpected behavior.

n0269.title: Allowing bugs and science
n0269.gist: Tolerating bugs can shorten low-level programs, and a bug that is a failure in engineering counts as a discovery in science, which is how ruliology has progressed.
